sections.title: The Fifth Plague: Livestock Diseased
observations: In this section, God strikes the livestock of the Egyptians, causing a severe loss to their economy and livelihood. This plague serves as a direct challenge to the Egyptian gods, particularly Hathor, the goddess of fertility and motherhood, who was often depicted as a cow.

The distinction made between the livestock of the Israelites and that of the Egyptians highlights God's protection over His people, reinforcing the theme of divine sovereignty and judgment against false gods.

sections.title: The Sixth Plague: Boils
observations: The introduction of boils on the Egyptians and their animals signifies a deepening of God's judgment. This plague not only affects the physical health of the Egyptians but also serves to humiliate the Egyptian magicians, who are unable to replicate or counteract this plague.
The physical affliction symbolizes the spiritual condition of Egypt, illustrating the consequences of hardening one's heart against God.

sections.title: The Seventh Plague: Hail
observations: The hailstorm is one of the most devastating plagues, demonstrating God's power over nature. It serves as a warning to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, showing that their refusal to heed God's commands will lead to severe consequences.
The mention of a few Egyptians who heed the warning and bring their livestock indoors illustrates the possibility of repentance and obedience, even amidst judgment.

importantVerses.commentary: God makes a distinction between His people and the Egyptians, emphasizing His protective nature and the consequences of sin.
God's purpose in raising up Pharaoh is to demonstrate His power and proclaim His name throughout the earth, highlighting the sovereignty of God in human affairs.
Pharaoh's acknowledgment of sin and request for prayer shows a moment of recognition of God's authority, yet his heart remains hardened, illustrating the struggle between repentance and rebellion.

questions: What do the plagues reveal about God's character and His relationship with His people?
How does the distinction between the Israelites and Egyptians in the plagues inform our understanding of God's justice and mercy?
In what ways does Pharaoh's response to the plagues reflect the human tendency to harden one's heart against God?
